questions.question: What is the purpose of the `useEffect` hook in React?
choices: Let you connect to an external system.
Let you update state based on previous state from an effect.
Let you display different content on the server and the client.
Let you synchronize a component with an external system.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the first choice because the passage states that `useEffect` lets you synchronize a component with an external system.
questions.evidence: useEffect is a React Hook that lets you synchronize a component with an external system.
questions.heading: useEffect – React

questions.question: What is the purpose of an Effect in React?
choices: To keep a component synchronized with an external system
To update a component's state when its parent changes
To trigger a component's render when its children change
To make a component re-render when its props change
questions.explanation: The passage states that an Effect lets you keep your component synchronized with some external system
questions.evidence: An Effect lets you keep your component synchronized with some external system (like a chat service).
questions.heading: useEffect > Usage > Note

questions.question: What should you do to prove to the linter that serverUrl doesn't need to be a dependency in the useEffect hook?
choices: Move serverUrl inside the component
Add serverUrl to the dependencies
Move serverUrl out of the component
Remove serverUrl from the dependencies
questions.explanation: You need to move serverUrl out of the component to prove it's not reactive and won't change on re-renders
questions.evidence: const serverUrl = 'https://localhost:1234'; // Not a reactive value anymorefunction ChatRoom({ roomId }) {  useEffect(() => {    const connection = createConnection(serverUrl, roomId);    connection.connect();    return () => connection.disconnect();  }, [roomId]); // ✅ All dependencies declared  // ...}
questions.heading: useEffect > Usage > Specifying reactive dependencies

questions.question: What happens to the dependency array in the useEffect hook when the createOptions function is created inside the Effect itself?
choices: The dependency array is not updated at all
The dependency array is updated every time the component re-renders
The dependency array is updated every time the createOptions function is called
The dependency array is updated only when the roomId changes
questions.explanation: The dependency array is updated only when the roomId changes
questions.evidence: function ChatRoom({ roomId }) {  const [message, setMessage] = useState('');  function createOptions() { // 🚩 This function is created from scratch on every re-render    return {      serverUrl: serverUrl,      roomId: roomId    };  }  useEffect(() => {    const options = createOptions(); // It's used inside the Effect    const connection = createConnection();    connection.connect();    return () => connection.disconnect();  }, [createOptions]); // 🚩 As a result, these dependencies are always different on a commit  // ...
questions.heading: useEffect > Usage > Removing unnecessary object dependencies

questions.question: Why does the author suggest replacing useEffect with useLayoutEffect in certain cases?
choices: Because it must block the browser from painting the screen
Because it runs before the browser paint
Because it's a more efficient effect
Because it's a more secure effect
questions.explanation: Because it must run before the browser paint
questions.evidence: You’ll only need this if it’s crucial to run your Effect before the browser paint: for example, to measure and position a tooltip before the user sees it.
questions.heading: useEffect > Troubleshooting > My Effect does something visual, and I see a flicker before it runs

questions.question: What is the first step in the branching and merging workflow described in the passage?
choices: Switch to your production branch.
Create a branch for a new user story.
Do some work in that branch.
Do some work on a website.
questions.explanation: The passage states that the first step is to do some work on a website.
questions.evidence: Do some work on a website.
questions.heading: Git - Basic Branching and Merging

questions.question: What happens to your project working directory when you switch to a new branch in Git?
choices: Git deletes all files in your working directory
Git resets your working directory to the branch's last commit
Git creates a new copy of your working directory
Git adds, removes, and modifies files to make your working copy look like the branch's last commit
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the first one, as the passage states that Git resets your working directory to look like it did the last time you committed on that branch.
questions.evidence: It adds, removes, and modifies files automatically to make sure your working copy is what the branch looked like on your last commit to it.
questions.heading: 3.2 Git Branching - Basic Branching and Merging > Basic Branching and Merging > Basic Branching

questions.question: What is the command to merge the `iss53` branch into the `master` branch?
choices: git merge master
git merge iss53
git pull iss53
git checkout iss53
questions.explanation: The correct command is to run `git merge iss53`.
questions.heading: 3.2 Git Branching - Basic Branching and Merging > Basic Branching and Merging > Basic Branching

questions.question: What happens to files with merge conflicts that haven't been resolved?
choices: Git adds standard conflict-resolution markers to the files
Git ignores them
Git marks them as unmerged
Git adds them to the commit
questions.explanation: The passage states that files with merge conflicts that haven't been resolved are listed as unmerged.
questions.evidence: Git adds standard conflict-resolution markers to the files that have conflicts, so you can open them manually and resolve those conflicts.
questions.heading: 3.2 Git Branching - Basic Branching and Merging > Basic Branching and Merging > Basic Merge Conflicts

questions.question: What happens to the commit message after you type git commit to finalize the merge commit?
choices: It is automatically filled in with the branch name and conflict information.
It is ignored and an empty message aborts the commit.
It is displayed to you for review before being committed.
It is modified to include details about how you resolved the merge.
questions.explanation: The commit message is displayed to you for review before being committed.
questions.evidence: # It looks like you may be committing a merge.
questions.heading: 3.2 Git Branching - Basic Branching and Merging > Basic Branching and Merging > Basic Merge Conflicts

questions.question: What is the return value of the fetch() function?
choices: A URL that is fulfilled with a Request object
A Request object that is fulfilled with a URL
A Response object that is fulfilled with a Promise
A Promise that is fulfilled with a Response object
questions.explanation: The fetch() function returns a Promise that is fulfilled with a Response object
questions.evidence: The fetch() function returns a Promise which is fulfilled with a Response object representing the server's response.
questions.heading: Using the Fetch API

questions.question: What happens to header names when using a Headers object?
choices: They are normalized to uppercase
They are not normalized
They are normalized to lowercase
They are not changed
questions.explanation: The passage states that the Headers object normalizes header names to lowercase.
questions.evidence: For example, it normalizes header names to lowercase, strips leading and trailing whitespace from header values, and prevents certain headers from being set.
questions.heading: Using the Fetch API > Making a request > Setting headers

choices: Pass the object to fetch() with options and change some properties
Pass the object to fetch() with options
Pass the object to fetch() directly
Pass the object to fetch() with options and create a new request from it
questions.explanation: You can create a request from another request, while changing some of its properties

questions.question: What happens if you call the Response.json() method on a response that can't be parsed as JSON?
choices: The method returns a Promise that will be fulfilled with the response status.
The method returns a Promise that will be rejected with an error.
The method returns a Promise that will be fulfilled with the response body.
The method throws a TypeError.
questions.evidence: The method will throw an exception if the response body is not in the appropriate format: for example, if you call json() on a response that can't be parsed as JSON.
questions.heading: Using the Fetch API > Handling the response > Reading the response body

questions.question: Why must you call Response.clone() before reading the body of a response more than once?
choices: Because the response is not yet fully received.
Because the response is locked and disturbed by another thread.
Because the response is not yet fully processed.
Because you need to read the body twice.
questions.explanation: Because the response is locked and disturbed by another thread.
